title: Municipal Trade Crews as Robot Training Data
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics & physical automation x Government/defense/municipal
one_liner: A cooperative that licenses consented, privacy-scrubbed first-person footage of city public-works and utility crews doing real skilled work to robotics labs, with revenue shared to the city and the union's training fund.
customer: Robotics foundation-model labs and robot-data buyers pay per usable hour (Physical Intelligence-class labs, XDOF, Mecka). The supply side is public works departments, transit maintenance shops and public-sector union locals (AFSCME, IBEW), which receive a 40-50% share.
problem: The humanoid bottleneck is a 'dearth of physical-world data'. Robot-data startups pay people to film themselves making coffee or fixing cars (XDOF at about $50M annualized revenue three months out of stealth, Mecka projecting $100M ARR). Those demos are shallow next to expert skilled-trade work in messy environments: valve exercising, hydrant flushing, pothole patching, streetlight repair, sewer inspection. Cities meanwhile face tight budgets and need non-tax revenue.
solution: Equip volunteer crews with head cameras and simple sensors for specified tasks. Scrub faces and license plates on-device, label task steps, and license clean hours under a contract in which the city retains ownership. Worker pay per hour and a union-controlled training fund keep labor onside. Later, offer 'task-specific corpora' by trade (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) via apprenticeship programs.
why_now: Robot foundation models raised at $3-14B valuations in 2026 and are starved for data. Data-as-a-service is the hot new category (XDOF, Mecka). The humanoid shipment wave (about 22,000 in H1 2026) creates immediate demand. Cities are under budget pressure (Maryland's new IT tax raised 77% less than projected).
revenue_model: Data licensing per usable hour and per task-specific corpus, with 40-50% of revenue shared to the city and union training fund. Enterprise annual data licenses for labs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for physical AI is expert skilled-trades demonstrations, and public works departments and their unions are the only large organized pools of trained workers with a single governance body that can sign one contract. Paying the workers and the union turns what looks like 'training your replacement' into a data dividend.
first_30_days: Find one mid-size public works department and one union local. Run a 10-worker, 2-week pilot with head cameras on two task types. Sell the first 300-500 cleaned hours to one robotics lab and pay the crews and training fund on the first invoice.

title: Certification-Ready OS for Sober Living Operators
one_liner: Software and audit-readiness for independent recovery residences, so the good operators become visible, certified and eligible for opioid-settlement and referral funding.
customer: Independent sober living and recovery residence operators (8-40 beds), who pay a monthly subscription. Counties, states and treatment programs later pay for verified-quality dashboards.
problem: Sober living is a largely informal industry with a few notorious bad actors. States are moving to certification, and funding streams increasingly require it. Good small operators run on spreadsheets and can't prove house rules, incident handling, naloxone logs, drug-testing policies and fair-housing compliance. Funders and hospital discharge planners can't tell who is real.
solution: A recovery-residence operating system built around the NARR standard and each state's certification rules. It covers rent and bed management, house-rule acknowledgments, incident and naloxone logs, drug-test policy records, complaint handling and resident outcomes. It has a gap assessment and mock certification audit, and generates an audit binder. A separate funder dashboard reports verified occupancy and quality metrics.
why_now: Ohio made certification mandatory in January 2025, and Virginia followed in July 2025. New York launched its first recovery residence certification program in early 2025. Certification has become a gatekeeper for state opioid-response subawards, opioid-settlement contracts and Medicaid reimbursement in some states. The SUPPORT reauthorization signed December 1, 2025 extended HUD's Recovery Housing Program and SAMHSA grants through FY2030.
revenue_model: $199-499 per house per month for the operating system. $1,500-3,000 certification-prep packages. Annual license fees from counties, health plans or opioid-settlement administrators for verified-bed and quality dashboards. Do not take pay-per-referral fees: federal and state patient-brokering laws (such as EKRA) make that dangerous.
non_obvious_insight: The gray market's problem is invisibility as much as bad operators: funders have no cheap way to tell good houses from bad. The trusted data trail is the product. The business model rule is to sell software to operators and dashboards to funders, and never take referral commissions. That keeps the network legally clean and trusted by courts, hospitals and families, which is what makes it hard to copy.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a new certification mandate (Ohio or Virginia). Offer 10 operators a free gap assessment against the NARR standard through state recovery-housing associations. Convert them to a $199/month readiness plan. Meet the state certifying body to align templates. Pitch one county opioid-settlement administrator on a pilot verified-bed dashboard.

title: Scrap-to-Tab: Supply-House Credit for Trade Scrap
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing shortage/trades labor/home services x Waste/recycling/circular economy/critical minerals/materials
one_liner: A weekly scrap-and-refrigerant buy-back inside independent HVAC, plumbing and electrical supply houses that pays contractors in credit against their supply-house tab.
customer: Independent supply houses (channel, and they benefit from lower receivables) and their solo-to-10-tech contractor accounts. Downstream buyers are scrap mills, refrigerant reclaimers and rare-earth/copper processors.
problem: Small trades are cash-starved: 1 in 5 subs waits 60+ days to be paid, and residential HVAC shipments fell 25-50% in 2025 with equipment prices about 40% above 2020. Techs burn hours hauling old coils and copper to yards, or leave value in the dumpster. Supply houses carry the credit risk on 30-60 day terms.
solution: At the counter: sorted bins, a certified scale and basic grading. Contractors drop copper, brass, aluminum coil, old compressors/motors and recovered refrigerant (handled via a licensed reclaimer). Credit posts to their account, or cash is paid minus a small fee. We settle with the supply house in cash monthly, which cuts its receivables, and sell graded loads. Later add a bounty for magnet-bearing inverter compressors and motors, sold to rare-earth recyclers.
why_now: The HFC phase-down keeps cutting virgin refrigerant, making recovered gas strategic. The Aug 2026 BIS rule shows scrap is now a national-security asset and 'may add materials'. Hyperscalers are pulling rare earths out of waste streams. The HVAC trough is squeezing small-shop cash.
revenue_model: 10-20% spread on scrap; per-pound fee on refrigerant; supply-house sponsorship; rare-earth magnet bounty.
non_obvious_insight: The supply counter is the only place every small trade shows up weekly, it already extends credit, and it is a natural sorting checkpoint. Scrap value paid as tab credit is working capital the supply house wants (lower receivables) and contractors value more than yard cash.
first_30_days: Sign two independent supply houses in one metro. Place a scale and six bins. Buy at about 85% of local yard price for 30 days, then sell to a yard and a reclaimer. Measure pounds per week and receivables reduction, and pitch other houses on days-sales-outstanding improvement.

title: Satellite Settlement Radar for Condo Buildings
one_liner: Use free satellite radar archives to give condo boards a 10-year movement history of their building, and turn it into litigation-grade evidence when a neighboring construction project caused the settlement.
customer: Florida condo associations and property managers (3+ story buildings under post-Surfside milestone and reserve-study rules), structural engineers doing milestone inspections (white-label), buyers' agents, lenders and insurers.
problem: Milestone inspections and reserve studies are snapshots, while settlement is a trend. Boards face assessments of $30k to $100k+ per unit and don't know whether nearby construction is moving their building. A University of Miami-led study of Sentinel-1 data found subsidence of up to 8 cm in the Sunny Isles and Surfside area between 2016 and 2023 and linked it to nearby construction, yet no local product turns that into building-level reports for boards.
solution: A six-page Settlement Screening Report per building. Run open-source InSAR pipelines on Sentinel-1 (and newer radar sources) for large-footprint or tall buildings, overlay neighboring construction permits and pile-driving dates, and flag movement trends and differential settlement. Engineers can rely on it as a screening input. Optional monthly monitoring, and a litigation package with a geodesy expert declaration for claims against adjacent developers.
why_now: Post-Surfside laws now force inspections and funded reserves, so boards are spending on engineers. Free multi-year radar archives and mature open-source processing (ASF HyP3, MintPy) mean a two-person team can process buildings retroactively. Incumbents (engineers, inspectors, insurers) have not integrated satellite evidence.
revenue_model: $750 to $2,500 per building per year, $300 wholesale per building for engineering partners, monitoring subscriptions, and contingency or expert fees on construction-damage claims.
non_obvious_insight: The archive already recorded the history, so on day one you can hand a board a decade of movement. The money is in the claim, not the report: construction-induced settlement is an insurable, litigable harm, and radar time series with permit overlays date the cause. Sell the report as the intake funnel for claim work with construction-defect counsel.
first_30_days: Process 50 buildings along the Miami Beach to Sunny Isles corridor with open tools and publish a free hotspot map. Contact 100 condo boards and 10 structural engineering firms. Sell five reports at $750 and sign one construction-defect litigator as a partner. Note the limits (resolution favors large buildings) in every report.

title: Assay-Verified Swarf Pooling for Machine Shops
one_liner: Turn the chip bin into a revenue line: two-bin alloy segregation, assayed weekly pickup, and pooled truckloads sold direct to mills and remelters.
customer: Ohio job shops and mid-size plants (20-300 employees) machining stainless, nickel alloys, titanium, brass or tool steel, especially aerospace, energy and medical suppliers. The first buyer is the plant manager or owner. A second buyer is any prime or OEM that wants a closed-loop 'revert' chain-of-custody.
problem: The chip bin is the only place in a shop where money leaves blind. Most shops tip all chips into one roll-off. The scrap yard grades by eye or its own XRF and pays a mixed-lot price. One shovel of aluminum in 316 stainless, or too much cutting oil, can drop the price by 30%-70%, while clean, segregated titanium and nickel-alloy turnings sell at multiples of mixed scrap. Nobody at the shop has time to sort, and small volumes are too tiny for mills to accept directly.
solution: 'SwarfStack': color-coded, RFID-tagged two- and three-bin systems in the shop, plus a weekly route truck with an onboard scale and a handheld XRF that assays each pickup and logs photo, weight, alloy and oil content to a shared ledger. A centrifuge or briquetter handles the oil. Pool by alloy across dozens of shops into full truckloads sold directly to mills, foundries and remelters. Pay the shop 70%-80% of net price and issue a digital scrap certificate for chain-of-custody. The provenance data becomes more valuable as metals tariffs increasingly reward proof of where metal was melted.
why_now: Reshoring is adding domestic machining hours, and with them chips. Metals lead times and alloy volatility keep prices high. The April 2026 Section 232 rewrite taxes the full customs value of metal derivatives and gives better treatment to U.S.-melted content, so provenance now has a price. Used handheld XRF analyzers now cost about what a used pickup does, and cheap vision models can identify alloy family from a photo of a bin.
revenue_model: A 20%-30% spread between the pooled sale price and what the shop is paid, plus $150-$300 per month bin and route fees, plus a small fee per digital scrap certificate. A route with 60 shops averaging $1,500 per month of chip value nets about $250k-$400k per year, before adding a briquetting and coolant-recovery arm.
non_obvious_insight: The scrap dealer's edge is not market power, it is that the shop does not know what is in its own bin. The metal was worth far more than the 'mixed' price, and shops give away five-figure sums each year without ever seeing the invoice line.
first_30_days: Buy a used handheld XRF for about $15k-$25k and rent a pickup with a platform scale. Sign 8 aerospace and medical suppliers in one county, starting with those cutting titanium, Inconel or stainless. Run pickups, assay each load, and send each shop a 'you left $X in your bin' statement showing the uplift against their current dealer. Pre-sell pooled loads to one stainless remelter and one titanium remelter before the first truckload.

title: Local-Law Radar for Data Center and Battery Developers
one_liner: A system that continuously reads city and county codes, planning agendas and minutes nationwide and warns developers which jurisdictions are drafting moratoria or new setback, noise and fire-safety rules before they pass.
customer: Land-acquisition and permitting teams at data-center, battery-storage, solar, EV-charging and peaker developers, siting consultants, and law-firm land-use groups.
problem: Local ordinances decide whether $100M-$1B projects get built, but roughly 19,000 municipalities publish codes and agendas as PDFs on inconsistent sites. Opposition-driven moratoria appear with weeks of notice, developers learn about them after buying land options, and existing zoning datasets capture setbacks and floor-area ratios, not conditional-use or moratorium rules for new infrastructure types.
solution: A scraper and LLM pipeline over municipal-code hosts and agenda platforms (Legistar, CivicClerk, PrimeGov and similar) that classifies items by project type, alerts on early signals ('first reading', 'study session', 'interim urgency ordinance'), answers 'is X permitted at parcel Y and under what conditions?', and scores county risk. Two land-use paralegals curate the output.
why_now: Data-center and battery-storage siting fights surged through 2025-26, including after the Jan 2025 Moss Landing battery fire (background, verify), and LLMs can now read messy municipal PDFs cheaply enough to cover thousands of jurisdictions.
revenue_model: $2-10k/month per developer team, $60-250k/year enterprise plans, and $500-2,000 per-parcel reports.
non_obvious_insight: Moratoria are telegraphed weeks ahead in public agendas that nobody reads at scale, so the value is the leading indicator, not the code text. A stranded land option costs far more than the subscription.
first_30_days: Cover the three states with the most data-center activity and track about 500 jurisdictions' agendas. Publish a weekly free moratorium tracker, sell five developers or site-selection consultants at $2.5k/month, and back-test which past moratoria would have been flagged 30 days early.

title: Solar Defection Radar for African Utilities
one_liner: Africa's invisible solar and battery boom leaves utilities, banks and insurers blind, so measure it district by district.
customer: African distribution utilities and regulators, development finance institutions, commercial banks and insurers.
problem: Africa installs 17 GW in 2026 (+45%), 75% of it distributed. Ember's estimates are 2x official figures, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Utilities cannot see which paying customers are leaving, and lenders cannot price the assets.
solution: Estimate installed solar and battery stock per district from customs and import data, rooftop detection in satellite imagery and installer sales data. The wedge is a quarterly district-level report for Nigeria or Kenya, sold to one utility and one DFI.
why_now: Chinese exports hit records and batteries now outsell panels in import dollars. Ember's 'invisible boom' finding is public but nobody has productised it.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per institution, plus bespoke studies for DFIs.
non_obvious_insight: When self-generation outruns official statistics, the first credible dataset becomes the reference for tariffs, credit and insurance pricing.
first_30_days: Combine public Chinese export data, Ember figures and roof imagery for Lagos and Kano. Give a free sample to three utilities and one DFI.

title: Universal Depot Operator for Stacked EPR Programs
one_liner: One neutral drop-off depot per town that serves batteries, paint, oil containers, textiles and small e-waste for many producer responsibility programs at once.
customer: PROs and stewardship programs (Circular Action Alliance, battery, paint and other stewardship organizations) under a master service agreement, plus host sites paid a host fee.
problem: EPR programs multiply, each building its own thin collection network. Colorado's Interchange 360 (petroleum containers) diverted about 2,500 lb in six months across 10 collection facilities, roughly 250 lb per site. Unit costs per pound are absurd, host sites drown in per-program rules, and households face a different trip per program.
solution: A shared depot at transfer stations and hardware stores with one trained staff, fire-safe cabinets and one weekly consolidated pickup. It is operated under a multi-PRO contract paid per pound plus a site fee. It starts in Colorado and Oregon and adds streams as new programs launch (California's SB 501 medium-format batteries, textiles).
why_now: Colorado's programs are just moving from planning to practice. Oregon's EPR survived the Commerce Clause challenge (Aug 2026) even as NAW appeals, and CAA collected $145.5M in 2025 while spending $56.5M, so budget exists to solve collection cost.
revenue_model: Per-lb handling fees and per-site fees from multiple PROs, host-fee share, and minor resale of recovered commodities.
non_obvious_insight: EPR is designed by material stream but households experience it by trip. The missing layer is a neutral aggregator that turns N programs into one drop-off and one truck.
first_30_days: Meet PRO operations leads in Colorado and Oregon. Pick 3 host sites in one county (a transfer station and 2 hardware stores). Price cabinets and a pickup route. Sign one PRO pilot on cost-plus terms.

title: Certified Raw Milk: Testing, Herdshares, Insurance
one_liner: The neutral assurance layer for the gray-legal raw milk market: weekly pathogen and H5N1 testing, herdshare paperwork, and the first insurable 'tested farm' program.
customer: Small dairies (roughly 5-100 cows) that sell raw milk through herdshares or state-permitted on-farm sales. Later, surplus-lines insurers and MGAs, and consumers who scan a batch QR code.
problem: Demand for raw milk is rising with the wellness and MAHA-era food politics, but farms run with no shared safety standard, no liability coverage, and thin legal paperwork. Herdshares are a legal workaround that state attorneys general and FDA (on interstate sales) increasingly scrutinize as disguised retail. H5N1 in dairy herds since 2024 and USDA's national milk-testing strategy raised the stakes. One sick customer can end a farm.
solution: A subscription with four parts. (1) Scheduled bulk-tank sampling, with a partner state-accredited lab running a pathogen panel (Salmonella, Listeria, STEC, Campylobacter) plus H5N1 PCR. (2) A public farm page and batch QR code that show results, including failures. (3) State-specific herdshare agreements and an incident-response protocol, reviewed by counsel. (4) After 6-12 months of data, a group liability policy priced off each farm's test history.
why_now: H5N1 in US dairy cattle (2024-26) made pathogen testing a mainstream topic. Federal and state milk-testing programs are expanding. Raw milk politics are at a high, and 2026 reporting shows FDA pressure on interstate sales and closer AG review of herdshare contracts. Farms now need a defensible paper trail, and insurers have no data to price this risk.
revenue_model: $150-400 per farm per month for testing and certification, with lab costs around 40%. Per-batch certificate fees. A 10-15% commission or MGA fee on group liability premiums once claims data exists. Optional $5/month 'verified member' fee paid by herdshare customers.
non_obvious_insight: Raw milk's growth is capped by trust and insurability, not demand. Insurers, retailers and regulators won't touch it because nobody can prove anything. The winner is not a milk brand but the certifier (think UL or organic certification) that publishes failures. Believers and skeptics can both trust that, and the test history becomes the underwriting dataset that unlocks insurance, which is the real moat.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a strong raw-milk farmer network and clear legal footing (for example Pennsylvania or Utah). Recruit 10-15 farms through state raw-milk associations and Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund events. Sign a wholesale rate with an accredited lab. Sell a $199/month 'weekly test plus public results page' pilot. Show 3 months of data to 2 surplus-lines brokers to scope a group liability program.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.

title: Designed Toxin Binders for Mouse-Free Antivenom QC
one_liner: Sequence-defined, AI-designed toxin-class binders sold as reference reagents that let antivenom makers test potency without mouse lethality assays.
customer: Antivenom manufacturers (public institutes in Latin America and India, plus private and UK/US firms), WHO and regulator working groups, toxinology labs, and funders such as Wellcome and Gates for later recombinant antivenom.
problem: WHO's 2017 guidelines say murine LD50 and ED50 lethality tests remain the only validated preclinical potency method, despite 3Rs pressure. ELISA, nAChR-binding and cytotoxicity surrogates exist but lack stable, defined, universal reagents, because animal-derived antibodies vary lot to lot.
solution: Produce designed binders for the major toxin families (three-finger toxins, PLA2, SVMP) in E. coli, following the approach in Nature (Jan 2025), where de novo proteins neutralized three-finger toxins and protected mice. Sell (1) calibrator and capture-reagent kits for competition ELISA and nAChR-competition assays, and (2) a 'toxin-family neutralization profile' service showing what each antivenom lot neutralizes, correlated to mouse ED50 over 10-20 lots. Later, co-develop recombinant cocktails.
why_now: The 2025 Nature paper proved designed proteins can neutralize venom toxins. WHO explicitly encourages alternatives. Regulators are moving toward non-animal methods (FDA's Sept 21, 2026 rule is the latest signal). AI design has made binders cheap.
revenue_model: $2-10k research-use kits, $5-20k per lot profile service, grants ($200k-2M) for validation, and later per-dose royalties on recombinant products.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames designed antivenom as a therapeutic moonshot. The wedge is quality control: reagents sell before regulators accept a replacement, and manufacturers already pay for mouse colonies. Sequence-defined reagents beat animal-derived ones on reproducibility. Honest caveat: first revenue is likely grants plus small reagent orders.
first_30_days: Check IP with the University of Washington and DTU or design new binders. Express three binders. Send sample sets to 2 antivenom labs for correlation on 10 lots. Apply for a small grant while selling research-use kits to toxinology labs.

title: Celebration-of-Life Concierge Using Restaurants' Dead Hours
one_liner: A flat-fee, turnkey memorial-gathering service for families who buy a cheap direct cremation and then have to improvise a goodbye, hosted in restaurants, breweries and hotel rooms during their empty weekday hours.
customer: Adult children (45-65) who bought direct cremation and must host 40-100 guests. Distribution partners are low-cost direct-cremation providers and hospice bereavement teams. Venues (restaurants, breweries, event rooms) pay a commission for filled dead hours.
problem: Funeral homes are hated for opaque upselling, so families flee to direct cremation at roughly $1,000-$3,000. That unbundles the ceremony: the gathering still happens 2-6 weeks later, but nobody provides it. Families scramble to find a venue, catering, a slideshow, an officiant and a livestream for remote relatives, while the cremation provider has no product for the moment that most shapes the family's memory of them.
solution: One booking that covers venue, per-head menu, host or officiant, memory-board and slideshow, RSVP and guest messaging, livestream and a printed program. The family pays a flat planning fee. The venue keeps the food and beverage revenue and pays a commission. Cremation providers and hospices embed a link in their after-care emails and take a referral fee or white-label it as their own add-on. A vetted list of local celebrants and photographers sits underneath.
why_now: The US cremation rate reached about 63.4% in 2025 and direct cremation is the fastest-growing disposition. NFDA reports that a majority of people have attended a funeral event at a non-traditional location, so the behavior has already shifted while the supply side is still a patchwork of ad hoc rentals. Restaurants and breweries are hunting for private-event revenue in weekday afternoons.
revenue_model: Family pays $750-$1,500 planning fee, plus add-ons (livestream, officiant, printed programs). Venue pays 12-15% of the food and beverage minimum (a 60-guest gathering at $55-$80 a head is $3-5k of spend). Referral fee of about $100 per booking to cremation providers and hospices.
non_obvious_insight: The funeral industry unbundled its own most emotional and highest-margin product. Disposition is now a commodity, but the ceremony did not disappear; it moved two to six weeks later, out of the funeral home, into a category no one owns, and it comes with a no-panic timeline, so the family is willing to plan and spend on it. The scarce resource is not a chapel, it is a trusted person who takes care of the whole afternoon.
first_30_days: Pick one high-cremation metro (Portland, Seattle, Las Vegas or Phoenix). Sign 8-10 venues with private rooms and per-head menus. Get two direct-cremation providers and two hospice bereavement coordinators to send a 'what happens next' link to families. Run the first gatherings by hand with a shared calendar, a phone line and a single landing page. The first paid bookings should come through partner referrals within weeks, and the service can stay fully concierge until 30-40 gatherings show what to automate.

title: SNAP-Ready Kits for Corner Stores
one_liner: A UPC-level 'variety counter' plus a pre-built wholesale fill kit that tells a convenience store exactly what to stock to keep SNAP authorization under USDA's new staple-food rule.
customer: Independent convenience stores, bodegas, small groceries and dollar-format stores that accept SNAP (USDA counts 269,217 authorized retailers, with small-format stores hit hardest). The store owner pays for the audit and kit. Secondary payers are the local cash-and-carry wholesalers and jobbers who earn incremental case sales, and city or state health departments that fund healthy-corner-store programs.
problem: USDA's final rule (effective July 7, 2026; implementation Nov 4, 2026) raises the stocking floor from 3 to 7 varieties in each of 4 staple categories (28 varieties), with 3 stocking units each (84 units) and perishables in 3 categories. The counting rules are counterintuitive: brown and white rice are one variety, all bread is one variety, and brands and flavors do not count. USDA's own analysis of 121,294 small-format stores found only 52% already stock enough dairy varieties and 63% enough protein, which implies roughly 58,000 stores short on dairy alone. Stores are assessed at reauthorization (every 5 years, about 54,000 stores a year) or at any time. Owners have no tool that tells them what to buy, and commenters said the rule is infeasible for small stores.
solution: An SMS and web tool. The owner uploads a POS export or photographs shelves. A classifier maps UPCs to USDA's variety groups, using the rule's Group 1 and Group 2 counting logic, and returns a gap list such as 'need 3 more dairy varieties and 2 more protein varieties, buy these SKUs'. A sold-through kit pre-negotiated with a local wholesaler uses the lowest-spoilage items that fit small refrigeration. The tool also produces a USDA evidence pack (dated photos, invoices, variety ledger) for reauthorization or a compliance review. A 'keep or drop SNAP' ROI calculator is built in, because most small stores earn little from SNAP.
why_now: USDA published the final rule on May 8, 2026 and the enforcement-ready implementation date is Nov 4, 2026, about five weeks out. The prior interim standard was only 3 varieties per category, so almost every small store has a gap to close. USDA also says it can assess any retailer at any time, and every store hits reauthorization within 5 years, so demand arrives as a rolling wave rather than a single date.
revenue_model: $79 one-time shelf audit, or free through wholesaler partners. Kit sold at wholesale plus a 10-15% margin, or a referral fee from the wholesaler. $29 per month monitoring with auto-reorder and evidence-pack refresh. Grant-funded 100-store packages ($500-1,500 per store) sold to health departments and food-access nonprofits. Anonymized gap data licensed to distributors.
non_obvious_insight: USDA admits it has no baseline data on how many stores fail, and its roughly $77M first-year cost estimate describes 'reviewing notice, guidance, and updating stock', which works out to a few hundred dollars per store. That looks far too low against stocking 28 varieties with perishables in tiny coolers, and commenters said so directly: 'refrigerated space is limited for perishable products... would lead to waste and higher operating costs' and 'stocking seven distinct grain varieties... is not feasible for small convenience stores'. Convenience stores are 44% of SNAP retailers but only 5% of redemptions and 76% of sanctions, so many owners will do the math and drop SNAP unless compliance is cheap and certain. The rule also leaves 'perishable' and 'stocking unit' undefined, which creates an interpretation gap that a shared variety ledger can fill. Evidence: final rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/08/2026-09137/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance and proposed rule https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/09/25/2025-18624/updated-staple-food-stocking-standards-for-retailers-in-the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance
first_30_days: Pick one metro with dense small-format stores. Sign one cash-and-carry wholesaler or jobber as the kit supplier. Encode the rule's variety-counting logic into a spreadsheet-based counter and walk 40 stores with a $79 audit, aiming for 15 paid audits and 5 kit orders. Publish a one-page 'what counts as a variety' guide and post it in grocer association WhatsApp and Facebook groups. Pitch the local health department a grant-funded 100-store pilot using the audit results as proof.

title: Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure
one_liner: A daily feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements to show who is quietly assembling land for data centers, solar and transmission weeks before anyone announces it.
customer: Competing data center, solar, storage and transmission developers' land teams and site-selection consultants; utility and co-op large-load planners; infrastructure and energy funds buying alternative data; and county economic development and planning offices wanting defensive visibility.
problem: Land assembly is a race, and the first public trace is a short memorandum of option, lease or easement recorded at the county. Nobody watches those at scale. The assessor doesn't reflect an unexercised option. The clerk's document-type field is a dropdown chosen by a data-entry clerk, so big deals hide under 'Other', 'Miscellaneous' or 'Agreement'. Developers find out about a competitor's 6,000 acres months late, counties learn from a leaked newspaper story, and everyone pays landmen $300-$600 a day to sit in vaults.
solution: Ingest recorded instruments from county portals and bulk feeds in target corridors. Classify by reading the full image, not the clerk's label. Cluster by grantee, signatory, notary, return-to law firm and mailing address to unmask LLC families. Flag assembly events, such as N option memos within X miles or easement clusters along a line that imply transmission or pipeline. Deliver alerts, a map, and parcel-level chain-of-title and existing-easement packets on demand, with a human landman reviewing the hard ones.
why_now: The 2025-2026 large-load land rush is real: options in Hallam, Nebraska are reportedly worth tens of thousands of dollars an acre, and Hill County, Texas land appraised near $7,100 an acre has been offered about $100,000 an acre. Options are documented only by memoranda under NDA. FinCEN's 2025 decision to exempt domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision finally reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $2k-$8k/month per regional developer or utility seat, $750-$2,000 per tract title packet, and $50k-$150k/year alt-data licenses for funds. Optional revenue share or free access for counties that provide bulk feeds.
non_obvious_insight: The return-to address and notary on a recorded memorandum are the fingerprint of the developer's counsel, and they reveal an assembly weeks before a rezoning hearing. The mislabeled document-type field is why nobody has done this with generic data vendors. Landmen are the recorder's best regulars and know exactly which counties are hot, which makes them the cheapest ground-truth labelers and first customers.
first_30_days: Choose two counties with a rumored project, pull 24 months of instruments, and build the classifier and clustering. Deliver a 'who is assembling where' memo free to 10 site-selection consultants and land brokers, then convert two into $3k-$5k pilots. Check each state's bulk-data commercial-use rules and offer the counties access to the same maps.

title: Parametric Lease-Up Delay Insurance
one_liner: Insurance that pays automatically if a public submarket days-to-lease index stays high during a building's lease-up, protecting developers' interest carry.
customer: Multifamily developers and construction and mezzanine lenders with 100-400 unit buildings in lease-up (1.2M units nationally), sold through debt brokers.
problem: Lease-up interest carry balloons when time-to-lease stretches (34 days, longest September since 2019, with concessions on 15.8% of stabilized units). Lenders demand reserves or personal guarantees, sponsors self-insure, and traditional delay-in-start-up cover only addresses physical damage.
solution: A parametric policy that pays a pre-agreed sum if an index of median days-to-lease or vacancy exceeds a strike for N months in the lease-up window. Priced with an actuarial model, backed by reinsurer capacity, and sold as carry cover or a lender-accepted replacement for personal guarantees.
why_now: Lease-up glut and tight balance sheets create demand, parametric infrastructure (fronting carriers, index data, automated payouts) has matured, and starts are down 15.5%, so risk may be front-loaded.
revenue_model: 6-10% rate on line on $1-5M limits, plus MGA commission and profit share.
non_obvious_insight: Developers cannot influence a submarket's days-to-lease, so it is transparent and free of fraud, which makes it insurable. Capacity providers can view this as a defined macro bet with a supply-starts-driven mean reversion, though correlation across deals is the key risk.
first_30_days: Build an index from public rent and vacancy data. Quote 10 hypothetical developer and lender deals. Partner with a parametric MGA or coverholder for risk-carrying capacity and sign one $500K-limit pilot.

title: Private Set Intersection Mule Graph for Credit Unions
one_liner: Let hundreds of small banks and credit unions ask 'has anyone flagged this payee account?' without revealing customers or lists, using cryptographic private set intersection.
customer: Credit unions and community banks, sold through CUSOs, leagues and core processors, plus fintech sponsor banks.
problem: One account takeover can send 50+ ACH transfers to accounts at multiple banks, and each bank sees only its slice. Large-institution consortia dominate, and smaller institutions avoid sharing because of privacy, liability and competitive-leakage worries, even though information-sharing rules (314(b)) allow it.
solution: A pre-payment check API and core-integration widget. A payee's hashed account and routing data is checked via private set intersection against the pool of accounts members have flagged, returning hit count, recency and fraud category without exposing either side's lists. It adds burst alerts that notify other members when a takeover is in progress and automates the compliance paperwork.
why_now: Open-source PSI libraries and confidential-compute services have matured. The FBI freeze data exposed the cross-bank blind spot, Socure's $5.2B valuation shows the market's value, and FedNow adoption is reaching smaller institutions.
revenue_model: $500-5K per month per institution by asset size, and per-check fees for fintechs.
non_obvious_insight: Banks decline to share data because of liability and competitive leakage, not indifference. Cryptography removes the objection without asking anyone to trust a vendor with their data, and the network effect is regional, so a single state league can seed it.
first_30_days: Talk to a state credit-union league and recruit 5 pilot credit unions. Seed with confirmed-fraud lists they already hold, build the API on open-source PSI, and sign letters of intent for paid rollout.

title: Builder Defect Outbreak Radar From Permit Clusters
one_liner: Epidemiology for houses: read repair-permit clusters by builder, subdivision and vintage to tell HOA boards they have a defect outbreak and how many months remain on the legal clock.
customer: HOA management companies and reserve-study firms (about $99-250 per community per year, or a $750 one-time scan). Independent home inspectors and buyer's agents in new-build subdivisions ($19-39 per address). Later, home-warranty companies and homeowners insurers as data licensees.
problem: Production-home defects (roofs, windows, stucco or siding, plumbing, foundations) show up as patterns, but each owner sees only their own house. Boards learn late. Statutes of repose and limitation for construction-defect claims typically run roughly 6-10 years depending on state and quietly expire. Buyers pay for the defect discount without knowing why, and the MLS says nothing.
solution: Ingest city and county permit data. Use an LLM to classify messy permit text (re-roof, window replacement, siding or stucco remediation, re-pipe, foundation or pier repair, water-intrusion repair). Tie parcels to subdivision, builder and year built from plat and assessor data. Compare repair-permit rates to age-matched control cohorts in the same metro. Flag statistically significant outliers. Deliver a 'Community Defect Scan': map, cohort comparison, estimated time left under the applicable state statute (information, not legal advice), and next steps (independent engineer, reserve study update, attorney consult). Also offer a per-address flag API for inspectors.
why_now: The 2020-2022 building boom, built under labor and material shortages with substitutions, is now 4-6 years old, when defects surface and the earliest repose clocks start closing. Permit portals and open data are far more digitized than five years ago. LLMs make classification of messy permit text nearly free. Insurers and lenders are increasingly sensitive to new-build condition.
revenue_model: Community scans at $750 one-time. Management-company portfolio subscriptions at $99-250 per community per year. Per-address inspector add-on at $19-39. Data licensing to warranty and insurance underwriters. Flat fees only, with no referral fees to law firms, to avoid fee-splitting problems.
non_obvious_insight: Individual defects are invisible, but outbreaks are not. Appraisers watch this pattern for years without a feed: neighbors all re-roofing in year 5, three permits for the same water-intrusion fix on one street. The payer isn't the buyer, it's the board with a ticking legal deadline and a manager who wants to look proactive. The trick that makes a 'builder X is an outlier' claim defensible is controlling for age, since old-house repairs are normal and only age-matched cohort comparison isolates the builder.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with clean open permit data and heavy 2019-22 production building (for example Denver suburbs, Phoenix East Valley or Austin/Round Rock). Build the pipeline over about 200 subdivisions. Produce 10 free scans for community managers. Have counsel review the wording (state permit counts and method only, no accusations). Pitch 5 management companies and 3 reserve-study firms, and sell the first 10 scans at $750.

title: Vendor Exit Desk for Fleets and Contractors
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that gets small fleets and home-service contractors out of predatory software and telematics contracts, and recovers the money the vendors keep billing.
customer: Owner-operators and fleets of 5-200 trucks locked into telematics or ELD contracts (Samsara, Motive). Also HVAC, plumbing and electrical contractors on ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber, and small property managers on AppFolio. The owner or office manager pays, and only out of money recovered or saved.
problem: These vendors sell month-to-month or 1-year terms, then enforce hidden multi-year renewals, exit fees, ship-date billing and auto-renew windows. Support is now AI-only, so the customer cannot reach a human who can fix it. One Samsara reviewer was charged $29,000 for a 3-year contract after negotiating 1 year. Another lost about $32,000 paying for unused devices for 1 year and 9 months. ServiceTitan customers report quoted exit fees of $22,000, $29,000 and $37,000. An AppFolio reviewer was billed a $1,290 cancellation fee and said cancelling took 4 months.
solution: The customer forwards the contract and 3 recent invoices. The service does six things. (1) Extract renewal dates and notice windows, then send certified-mail non-renewal notices on the right day. (2) Audit billing against reality: billing that started at ship date rather than install date, decommissioned trucks still billed, duplicate accounts, and charges after cancellation. (3) Build a dispute packet with the sales promises, the timeline, and a card-network chargeback filing where the payment was on a business card. (4) Negotiate with the vendor's retention or legal team, with a partner attorney handling demand letters so the desk does not practice law itself. (5) Handle the data export. (6) Refer the customer to a replacement vendor that pays a bounty for the switch.
why_now: The 1-2 star reviews are dated 2026. They show vendors under public-market pressure enforcing renewals and paywalling features, for example Samsara charging $10 per truck for a feature shown in the demo. They also show support moving to AI. A Housecall Pro review dated Sept 28, 2026 says 'No support unless you want to speak with AI', and a Tithe.ly reviewer says the same in Feb 2026. Customers have nobody to call, so a human escalation path is now something they will pay for.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered or avoided dollars, with no fee if nothing is recovered. A $199 flat billing audit for small accounts. A $300-$1,000 referral bounty from the competing vendor that wins each switched fleet or contractor. An optional $29 per vendor per year renewal-watch subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The leads identify themselves. Each reviewer posts the vendor, the dollar amount, the date and the grievance publicly, so the whole first-year pipeline is already listed. Evidence: Samsara ($29,000 3-year contract, $32,000 unused devices, $900/month billed from ship date, $10/truck feature paywall) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/samsara.com. ServiceTitan ($22K, $29K and $37K exit quotes) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/servicetitan.com. Motive (renewal-window traps, charged again after cancelling) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/gomotive.com. AppFolio ($1,290 fee, 4-month cancellation) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/appfolio.com. Housecall Pro (charged $189 three times after cancelling, price doubled from $351 to $681) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/housecallpro.com. The winning product is not software. It is a library of each vendor's contract clauses, notice windows and escalation paths, built up case by case, and it gets more effective with every dispute settled.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull the roughly 300 public 1-2 star reviews from the last 12 months across those 5 vendors and tag each by vendor, dollar amount and whether the customer is still active. Days 8-14: contact reviewers by the review reply or an email lookup, offering a free contract read. Sign a contract attorney on a small retainer. Days 15-30: take 5-10 contingency cases and publish 'how to cancel [vendor]' pages, since people search that phrase. Use the settled cases to build the clause library. Also pitch 2 competing telematics vendors on the switch bounty.

title: The Second Ceremony After Direct Cremation
one_liner: A scattering-day and celebration-of-life concierge for the majority of families who chose cremation with no service and later realize they need a ritual.
customer: Adult children aged 40 to 65, two to twelve months after a direct cremation of a parent. Channels: online direct-cremation providers, hospice social workers and estate attorneys.
problem: The NFDA projects a 63.4% US cremation rate for 2025, rising toward 82% by 2045, and direct cremation ($1,000 to $3,000, no viewing, no service) is the fastest-growing segment. Families later improvise: an urn in a closet, a scattering with unclear legality, a restaurant back room. Funeral homes make nothing on this, and direct-cremation providers do not offer events.
solution: Fixed-price packages. Scattering day: jurisdiction-specific permit and rule guidance, boat or site scouting, a celebrant, a biodegradable urn, photographer or drone, and a livestream for distant relatives. Celebration of life: venue, catering, an AI-assisted slideshow built from the family's photos, an officiant, a guestbook and thank-you notes. Keepsake add-ons such as glass, vinyl, reef or tree. A planner keyed to 'days since death' nudges families at 30, 60 and 90 days.
why_now: Direct cremation took off with online price comparison, and the NFDA's 2025 report finds most people (58.3%) have attended a funeral at a non-traditional location. AI makes the slideshow, program and eulogy drafting cheap. Cremation providers are looking for post-sale revenue and a 'what now' answer for customers.
revenue_model: $900 to $4,500 per event: a $500 to $1,200 coordination fee plus 15% to 25% margin on boats, venues and catering. A 10% to 15% referral share to cremation providers that embed the offer. Annual remembrance add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Direct cremation removed the ceremony from the funeral bundle, and the vacuum reappears months later when the buyer is calmer, has a longer planning horizon and pays for meaning rather than logistics. The unbundled piece is the second funeral, and it can be more profitable than the first because there is no legacy funeral-home cost base.
first_30_days: Choose a coastal city such as San Diego, Seattle or Boston. Contract two licensed boat charters, three celebrants and a photographer. Write one-page scattering compliance sheets for the local jurisdictions. Interview hospice social workers to find referrals, and offer 10 founding families a $650 scattering-day package. Ask two direct-cremation providers to link the offer from their post-cremation emails, and aim for five events by month three.

title: Dixie Flatline for Retiring Plant Operators
one_liner: Neuromancer's Dixie Flatline (a dead expert preserved as a consultable construct) built for retiring water and plant operators, with consent, clip-grounded answers and royalties paid to the expert.
customer: Municipal water and wastewater utilities, rural electric co-ops and small chemical or food plants, reached through state rural water associations and funded by state workforce and infrastructure grants.
problem: A large share of plant operators is nearing retirement, and the knowledge that matters is tacit ('when pump 3 hums like that in the cold, do this'). SOP binders miss it, experts sandbag because they fear being replaced, and a hallucinating chatbot is unacceptable when chlorine dosing is involved.
solution: A three-week Walkdown Capture: the expert tours the plant with a chest camera and mic, thinking aloud. Their answers are aligned with SCADA and alarm history so past incidents can be replayed ('what did you do in the January freeze?'). Structured critical-decision interviews feed a queryable construct that answers only with citations to the expert's own clips, deployed on a tablet or radio for night operators. The retiree signs a consent and royalty agreement, is paid per consult, can revoke, and remains reachable as a paid human escalation.
why_now: Utilities are in the middle of a retirement wave, and cheap wearable cameras, speech-to-text and retrieval systems make capture-and-query affordable for a small team. Regulators and grant programs increasingly fund workforce succession.
revenue_model: $20-45k per capture project, $1-3k per month hosting per plant, and a royalty share passed through to the expert.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not modeling but eliciting and compensating. Experts hide knowledge when the goal is replacement, and paying them a revocable royalty flips the incentive. Grounding every answer in the expert's own clips solves the hallucination problem and makes the tool defensible with regulators and insurers.
first_30_days: Ask three state rural water associations for introductions. Run one pilot with a retiring operator for $5k or free, and produce a short demo of a construct answering a night-shift question with clip evidence. Aim for three paid projects by month six.
